reference.source: Scriver's OMMBID / Nelson Textbook of Paediatrics
clinicalPearls: Autosomal recessive deficiency of the liver isoform (CPT1A) on the outer mitochondrial membrane, which conjugates long-chain fatty acids to carnitine so they can enter the carnitine cycle
Classically presents in infancy with fasting hypoketotic hypoglycaemia, hepatomegaly and Reye-like encephalopathy during intercurrent illness
Renal tubular acidosis has been described as a distinctive associated feature
Unusually among oxidation defects, plasma total and free carnitine are typically normal or elevated rather than low, with a very low ratio of long-chain acylcarnitines to free carnitine on screening
Cardiomyopathy and skeletal myopathy are characteristically absent because the muscle isoform is unaffected
A common CPT1A variant is highly prevalent in some Arctic Indigenous populations and is associated with hypoglycaemia and infant mortality risk during fasting
Management centres on strict avoidance of fasting, generous carbohydrate cover during illness and long-chain fat restriction with medium-chain triglyceride substitution
reference.pathophysiology: Carnitine palmitoyltransferase 1 sits on the outer mitochondrial membrane and catalyses transfer of long-chain acyl groups from coenzyme A to carnitine, the committed first step allowing long-chain fatty acids to be transported into the mitochondrion for beta-oxidation. Deficiency of the hepatic isoform blocks long-chain fat oxidation and hepatic ketogenesis during fasting, producing hypoketotic hypoglycaemia and hepatic dysfunction, while free carnitine accumulates because it is not being consumed to form acylcarnitines. The muscle and cardiac isoform being distinct, striated muscle is spared, distinguishing this disorder from CPT2 and translocase deficiencies.
additionalDifferentials: Very-long-chain and long-chain hydroxyacyl-CoA dehydrogenase deficiencies
Reye syndrome and other causes of infantile hepatic encephalopathy
Ketotic hypoglycaemia and glycogen storage disorders
additionalInvestigations: Plasma acylcarnitine profile showing high free carnitine with low long-chain acylcarnitines (raised C0/(C16+C18) ratio)
Plasma total and free carnitine (typically normal or elevated)
Blood glucose, ketones, ammonia, lactate and liver function during illness
Renal tubular function assessment for associated acidosis
CPT1A molecular genetic testing to confirm the diagnosis
Fibroblast enzyme assay where genotype is inconclusive
redFlags: Hypoketotic hypoglycaemia with reduced consciousness during fasting or illness
Acute hepatic dysfunction with hyperammonaemia (Reye-like presentation)
Recurrent decompensation triggered by intercurrent infection
Renal tubular acidosis complicating an acute crisis
reference.prognosis: With reliable avoidance of fasting and prompt treatment during illness the outlook is good and growth and development are usually normal; morbidity relates chiefly to hepatic crises precipitated by fasting or infection.
pitfalls: Being reassured by normal or high carnitine levels and dismissing an oxidation defect
Permitting prolonged fasting for procedures without glucose cover
Expecting cardiomyopathy or myopathy, whose absence does not exclude the diagnosis
references: Scriver's OMMBID (Online Metabolic and Molecular Bases of Inherited Disease)
